blocks.text: Binary search maintains an active ordered candidate interval that is known to contain every still-possible answer. A midpoint observation is useful only when the problem's order or predicate proves that one whole side cannot contain the required answer. Removing that side preserves the invariant and reduces the candidate count; input size, numeric type, and variable names provide no such proof.
Define exactly what mid tests, which region each result eliminates, and why every answer in that region is impossible. If either branch lacks that sentence, ordinary binary search is not justified.

blocks.text: If an interval of size n is reduced to at most about n/2 after every midpoint evaluation, after k iterations at most n/2^k candidates remain. Reaching one candidate requires k = Θ(log n). Names such as left, right, and mid do not establish that recurrence.

The interval updates must strictly exclude mid or otherwise prove progress. If one midpoint evaluation costs T(n), the search can cost Θ(T(n) log n), plus any preprocessing; logarithmic iteration count alone is not an O(log n) total-time proof.

blocks.text: Having a first true index is not enough. First-true binary search requires every earlier value to be false and every value from the boundary onward to remain true. The sequence false, true, false, true crosses the boundary three times, so a midpoint result cannot characterize a complete side.

At index 2 the predicate is false. Moving right because false supposedly means 'before the boundary' discards the actual first true at index 1. No midpoint formula can repair a non-monotonic predicate.

blocks.text: The search makes Θ(log W) predicate calls, each costing Θ(P(n)), so sequential work multiplies to Θ(P(n) log W), matching the offered O(P(n) log W) bound. The predicate and iterative search both use O(1) auxiliary space under the explicit constraints, and predicate-local storage is released between calls, so peak auxiliary space remains O(1).

Time O(log W) omits predicate cost, O(P(n)) omits repeated calls, and O(W·P(n)) is loose rather than tight. Space O(log W), O(P(n)), and O(W) contradict the stated iterative constant-state and constant-space predicate contracts.
